meta.location: Bountiful, the sea, and the promised land
meta.unit: Voyage to the promised land (1 Nephi 16–18)

world_behind.title: A ship not after the manner of men
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says "manner" four times, three of them negations: not learned by men, not after the manner of men, not after the manner of men, but "after the manner which the Lord had shown unto me" (v. 2). Ancient Arabian yards sewed their hulls with cord; whatever this design was, the record's whole interest in it is the drafting room it came from.

spans.text: after the manner which the Lord had shown unto me

world_behind.title: Two sons of the exile
world_behind.text: "The elder was called Jacob and the younger Joseph" (v. 7): desert-born boys named for the two patriarchs who died outside the promised land, Jacob in Egypt and Joseph in a coffin awaiting carriage home. Lehi names his wilderness sons as if to say: our family too will be buried toward a land it must be carried into.

spans.text: The elder was called Jacob and the younger Joseph

world_behind.title: Merriment was not the sin
world_behind.text: Israel danced and sang after the Red Sea; monsoon sailing has long calm stretches and idle hands. What the record indicts is the amnesia inside the party: they "did forget by what power they had been brought thither" (v. 9), and the "much rudeness" (v. 9) names speech that had slipped its reverence.

world_behind.title: Sick-beds on a deck
world_behind.text: Verse 18 lays Jacob's lament over Lehi and Sariah: grey hairs brought down low, this time toward "a watery grave" (v. 18). Aged parents, a rolling ship, four days of storm, and grief doing what the tempest could not: the scene's physical misery is easy to read past and shouldn't be.

world_behind.title: Driven back is a sailor's report
world_behind.text: A ship that "knew not whither they should steer" (v. 13) runs before the wind; being "driven back upon the waters for the space of four days" (v. 15) is what happens when no one can hold a course. The narrative's seamanship is exact: lose the helmsman, lose the heading, lose the sea-room.

world_behind.title: The arrival inventory
world_behind.text: Seeds from Jerusalem that "did grow exceedingly" (v. 24), forests carrying "both the cow and the ox, and the ass and the horse" (v. 25), and "all manner of ore, both of gold, and of silver, and of copper" (v. 25): the promised land is audited in a farmer-smith's categories, the same hands that tilled Bountiful's shipyard now counting its wealth.

words.text: Cut and shaped wood, the plural naming the finished pieces. The party "did work timbers of curious workmanship" (v. 1), and the Lord showed Nephi from time to time what manner of work to do on them. The record uses the word ten times and the King James Bible not at all; every other use is a fortification, the pickets and breastworks Moroni threw up around his cities (Alma 50:2-3, 53:4). Both jobs are the same one: building something that will hold under a force nobody can argue with.

words.text: "Did go into the mount oft, and I did pray oft unto the Lord" (v. 3): the adverb doubled, once for the climbing and once for the praying. The ship arrived as installments, shown "from time to time" (v. 1), and revelation in this chapter runs at the frequency of the asking. A single mountain visit builds no ship.

words.text: They "began to make themselves merry" (v. 9): the verb assigns the mood a manufacturer. Merriment that is made rather than given has to be maintained, and the maintenance (dancing, singing, rude speech) crowds out the one act the voyage required of its passengers, which was remembering.

words.text: First time the record gives the ball this name; chapter 16 knew only "the compass" (v. 12) as "the ball" and "the pointers." Alma will one day interpret Liahona as compass (Alma 37:38), but the name surfaces here, at the exact moment the thing stops: the instrument is named in its silence.

words.text: "The tempest began to be exceedingly sore" (v. 14): the old adverb for grievous. One verse later the word migrates from weather into flesh, wrists and ankles swollen and "great was the soreness thereof" (v. 15). The storm and the cords are one affliction, and the vocabulary knows it.

words.text: "We did begin to till the earth" (v. 24): the promised land is received with a farmer's verb. No conquest, no city, no altar scene survives into the record of arrival; tents are pitched, seeds go in, and the land of promise begins as a planted field.

phrases.term: After the manner which the Lord had shown unto me
phrases.text: Chapter 17 issued the promise ("after the manner which I shall show thee"); this clause reports it kept. The verse guards the point with three negations of human manner, and verse 3 supplies the mechanism: a builder who climbed and prayed oft. Revealed pattern plus repeated appointments equals a finished hull.

phrases.term: Did forget by what power they had been brought thither
phrases.text: The voyage's actual sin, stated as amnesia. Nobody denies the power; they lose track of it, and the slide runs from dancing to "exceeding rudeness" (v. 9) without a single decision to rebel. Forgetting, in this record, is the first motion of mutiny.

cites.quote: exceeding rudeness

spans.text: exceeding rudeness

phrases.term: Swallowed up in the depths of the sea
phrases.text: Three times in one chapter: feared by Nephi (v. 10), approached in fact ("we were about to be swallowed up in the depths of the sea" (v. 15)), and staring down the brothers when they finally repent (v. 20). The phrase is the voyage's pressure gauge, and it only releases when the cords come off.

cites.quote: we were about to be swallowed up in the depths of the sea

spans.text: we were about to be swallowed up in the depths of the sea

phrases.text: The record's careful verb for the binding: the Lord permitted it, "that he might show forth his power" (v. 11). Four days of a prophet's swollen wrists are allowed to run because a demonstration is in progress. Suffering in this theology can be instructional without being authored.

cites.quote: that he might show forth his power

spans.text: that he might show forth his power

phrases.text: The family's oldest verb, negated at last. Laman murmured at the start (1 Ne. 2:12), even Lehi murmured at the broken bow (16:20); here the man with the swollen wrists reports "I did not murmur against the Lord because of mine afflictions" (v. 16). The register the record has kept since the valley makes this its counter-entry.

cites.quote: I did not murmur against the Lord because of mine afflictions

spans.text: I did not murmur against the Lord because of mine afflictions

phrases.text: The clause Mark will use of Galilee (Mark 4:39), word for word, and the psalmist's "the winds did cease" (v. 21) sequence before it: prayer, then stillness. In both canons the calm outranks the storm as the display of power, and in both the question that follows is who this is that the sea obeys.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: A ship described only by what it was not
verses.text: The record gives three denials in one verse and no positive description: "I did not work the timbers after the manner which was learned by men, neither did I build the ship after the manner of men," and then, a third time, "it was not after the manner of men." Size, shape, rig, and hull are all absent. The one positive statement is about method, that the Lord "did show me from time to time after what manner I should work the timbers," and verse 3 supplies the mechanism, going into the mount and praying. A vessel that carries the whole family across an ocean is never once described.

verses.label: v. 6–7
verses.title: A boarding list interrupted by two births
verses.text: The record loads the ship by category: fruits, meat, honey, provisions, loading, seeds, "and whatsoever thing we had brought with us, every one according to his age." Then verse 7 stops the manifest to introduce two people who have not appeared before: "my father had begat two sons in the wilderness; the elder was called Jacob and the younger Joseph." Eight years of travel produced two children and the record mentions them for the first time at the moment the family leaves. Jacob will write a book; Joseph is named at 2 Nephi 3:1 and little else.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: The offence specified rather than summarized
verses.text: The record names three actions where a summary would do: they "began to dance, and to sing, and to speak with much rudeness." Only the third is stated as a fault, and the interpretation follows in the same sentence, "they did forget by what power they had been brought thither." The verse then repeats its own key word, closing on "they were lifted up unto exceeding rudeness," so the term that carries the judgment is used twice and the two neutral activities are left standing beside it.

verses.label: v. 12–15
verses.title: One clock read three times in four verses
verses.text: The record counts the days of the storm at each stage: driven back "for the space of three days" at verse 13, then "on the fourth day, which we had been driven back" at verse 14, then "after we had been driven back upon the waters for the space of four days" at verse 15. Three statements of elapsed time in a passage of four verses. Verse 13 also records a decision made under that pressure and not reversed, "nevertheless they did not loose me," which fixes the point at which fear alone was insufficient.

verses.label: v. 15
verses.title: Swelling recorded where nothing requires it
verses.text: The record supplies clinical detail: the bands come off the wrists "and behold they had swollen exceedingly; and also mine ankles were much swollen, and great was the soreness thereof." No argument in the chapter needs it, and verse 16 immediately moves to praise. Four days bound in a pitching hold is the kind of thing a summary drops, and this account keeps the injury and gives it its own clause.

verses.label: v. 17–20
verses.title: Five appeals listed, all of them recorded as failures
verses.text: The record itemizes what did not work before naming what did: the father's many words, the sons of Ishmael addressed, the parents brought down to their sick-beds, the two small children "having need of much nourishment," and Nephi's wife "with her tears and prayers, and also my children." Verse 20 then supplies the single sufficient cause: "there was nothing save it were the power of God, which threatened them with destruction, could soften their hearts." The list exists in order to be negated, and the family's grief is recorded in detail precisely because it changed nothing.

verses.label: v. 25
verses.title: A whole continent inventoried at one stroke
verses.text: The record lists what was found: cow, ox, ass, horse, goat, wild goat, "and all manner of wild animals," then gold, silver, and copper. Six named animals in three pairs and three metals, with the domestic pairs given before the wild. The verse also states when the finding happened, "as we journeyed in the wilderness," so the survey is placed after landing rather than at it. This is the fullest such list in these books; later inventories, at Ether 9:18–19 for instance, add names the record never explains.

chapter.title: The wilderness cycle, proven portable
chapter.text: Merriment for murmuring, cords for the bound prophet, a stopped compass for a broken bow, storm for hunger, repentance, deliverance: the sea voyage runs the exact loop the desert ran in chapter 16. The record is demonstrating that the pattern belongs to the people. Moving them onto a ship changed nothing about it.

chapter.title: The compass's negative proof
chapter.text: Chapter 16 stated the rule (works by faith and heed); chapter 18 proves it by subtraction: bind the man of faith and the needle dies mid-ocean. The instrument's stoppage is the record's cleanest demonstration that its guidance was never mechanical.

chapter.title: Suffering, permitted for display
chapter.text: "The Lord did suffer it" is a complete theology in five words: evil allowed, bounded, and conscripted into demonstration. The chapter neither blames God for the cords nor pretends he was absent while they cut; it holds the harder middle position.

chapter.title: The innocent pay first
chapter.text: The record lists the casualties of the binding by household position before it lists any injury to the man bound. Verses 17 and 18 give the parents "upon their sick-beds" and "near to be cast with sorrow into a watery grave." Verse 19 gives Jacob and Joseph, "being young, having need of much nourishment," and then "my wife with her tears and prayers, and also my children." Only at verse 15 does the record mention swollen wrists and ankles, and verse 16 records the bound man praising "all the day long." Five parties suffer before the one who is tied.

chapter.title: Praise is the anti-murmur
chapter.text: Verse 16 answers sixteen years of the family's signature verb with its opposite, performed under the conditions that best excuse murmuring. The record has been building this contrast since the valley of Lemuel, and it spends it here, on swollen wrists.

chapter.title: Authority returns without a speech
chapter.text: Loosed, Nephi takes the compass, prays, steers, and never once relitigates the binding. The ruler-complaint of verse 10 is answered by a man ruling nothing but the helm; the record lets competence and mercy make the argument that soberness could not.

chapter.title: The unit ends in soil
chapter.text: Three chapters of bows, forges, and rigging close with seeds in the ground and the family's third naming ("we did call it the promised land"). The voyage unit's last lesson is proportion: the miracle gets one verse of calm, and the covenant's fulfillment looks like farming.

applications.title: Go into the mount oft
applications.text: Whatever your ship is, its blueprint arrives in installments, at the frequency of your asking. Put the climbing on a schedule: same mount, repeated appointments, and let the design accumulate.

applications.title: Keep a brought-hither list
applications.text: The voyage's sin was the amnesia inside the celebration. Keep a running list of what power brought you to where you are, and read it before the occasions most likely to turn merry.

applications.title: Watch your instruments
applications.text: When guidance goes quiet, check first how the covenant things in your life are being treated: the counsel bound and gagged, the practice tied down. Compasses in this record stop for moral reasons before mechanical ones.

applications.title: Praise before analysis
applications.text: Nephi's first act with freed hands was praise, all day, before any accounting of the wrong. In the hours after your own bands come off, try his order of operations; the analysis will still be there, and it will be saner for having waited.

applications.title: Count the blast radius
applications.text: The brothers thought they were settling a score with Nephi; the bill went to their parents, their little brothers, and a sister-in-law. Before letting a quarrel run another week, list who is actually absorbing it. The list is rarely the opponent.

applications.title: Resume the helm without a speech
applications.text: After vindication, Nephi steered; he did not prosecute. When events prove you right, take up the work quietly and leave the relitigating to the storm that already made your case.

questions.text: What am I building that I have only visited the mount once about, and when is my next appointment?
In my current season of ease, what power am I at risk of forgetting, and what would remembering look like out loud?
Which sources of guidance in my life have gone still, and what have I bound that might explain the silence?
When my afflictions last eased, was my first hour praise or grievance, and what would it take to reverse the order?
Whose grey hairs are absorbing a conflict I am keeping alive, and what would loosing the cords cost me, really?
If my promised land arrived tomorrow, do my habits know how to plant it, or only how to sail?
